evidence: Fixtures landed in 5559474, 2026-08-09 16:53:10Z, already carrying Summitline 'Winter skills & gear | 9' and PeakPath 'Winter hiking | 4' (git show 5559474:<fixture> verified).
SKILL.md Step 9 at that same commit contained NO unavailable-input rule and no proxy example at all — it ended at 'Produce a final report with: Executive Summary, Prioritized Gap List …'.
The string 'competitor cluster depth' first enters SKILL.md and gap-analysis-frameworks.md in 3e63967, 2026-08-10 17:02:47Z, a day later (git log -S).

3e63967's own commit message states the motive: 'evals 1 and 3 state no tool is connected, and not one of the five fixtures carries a volume field' — the fix was authored while reading these fixtures.
fixture_example_fitting.consequence: This is ledger F18's mechanism operating through a new carrier: not the anti-slop ruleset but the skill body itself. SKILL.md:164 hands any executor of eval 1 (a) the proxy route, (b) the basis wording ('a coverage proxy, not a volume measurement') and (c) the exact arithmetic for this fixture's headline gap ('9 + 4 articles across the two competitors'). Executor A's e1 §7 reproduces all three: 'Search Demand is scored from combined competitor cluster depth … (winter 9 + 4 = 13 …). This is a coverage proxy, not a volume measurement.' Expectation e1.5's Search-Demand clause therefore cannot discriminate — a cold executor is told the answer by a required read. Executor B's e4 took the same route but built its own 5-band mapping of counts to scores, which is independent construction the skill does not supply, so e4 retains some discriminating power on this clause. The fix is F18's own: state the rule with a neutral illustration and move the fixture-derived arithmetic off the executor's required-read surface. Note that F18's clean list still names content-gap-analysis as unaffected; that is true of the ruleset vector only.
fixture_example_fitting.recommendation: Increment F18 and record content-gap-analysis as a sixth known-affected suite via the skill-body carrier.

family_8_read_e4.question: Is executor B's family-8 position defensible as written, independently of the coordinator's forthcoming ruling?
family_8_read_e4.read: DEFENSIBLE, with one internal inconsistency that is the real defect.
for: Family 8's harm model is stated as 'a skill slug, which names a tool in a library they do not have'. This prompt asserts the opposite twice — 'what happens next in your skills library' and 'so we can run that skill without re-explaining everything' — so the reader named by the prompt holds the library and asked for the handle. The harm the family names cannot arise for this reader.

Family 7, the sibling family, states the boundary as 'the test is the reader, not the section', and exempts 'surfaces read only by author or operator'. Family 8's exemption paragraph applies the same distinction ('whether the string denotes something the client can hold').

Every one of the eight occurrences is preceded by a plain-language 'Job:' line ('Job: validate search demand for four footwear sub-topics before any is written'), so family 8's prescribed remedy — name the job, never the artefact — is satisfied IN ADDITION to the handle, not instead of it. A reader without the library still has an actionable instruction.

The suite itself mandates the string: e4.1 requires the response to 'explicitly name keyword-research'. A slug-free deliverable fails e4.1. This is ledger F13-r4's second finding — a suite enforcing what a ruleset forbids — recurring on a second suite.
against: The section heading 'written for whoever runs the toolkit, not for the shop floor' is a section-level declaration, and family 7's wording says the section is precisely what does not decide the question. B's argument survives only because the PROMPT establishes the reader, not because the heading does — B should be read as resting on the prompt, and its own text does rest there.

The decisive weakness is inconsistency, not principle: having ruled its operator section may carry handles, B gave handles to three skills and withheld them from three others ('the writing job', 'the structured data job', 'the internal linking job'). The same operator gets a runnable handle for competitor-analysis and none for the writer skill they will need first. That inconsistency is what costs e4.2.

ungraded_defects.finding: e3 L214 states «Οι τίτλοι είναι προτάσεις προς επεξεργασία από τους φυσικοθεραπευτές σας. Κανένας δεν αντιγράφει τίτλο ανταγωνιστή.» (none copies a competitor title). Mechanically checked against the fixture: 9 of the 14 proposed titles open with a competitor article title verbatim and append a colon-subtitle — «Ρήξη μηνίσκου: συντηρητική αντιμετώπιση» + «χωρίς χειρουργείο»; «Πρόληψη πτώσεων στο σπίτι» + «τι αλλάζουμε σε κάθε δωμάτιο»; «Αυχενικός πόνος από το κινητό» + «γιατί εμφανίζεται…»; «Φυσικοθεραπεία μετά από κάταγμα ισχίου», «Ασκήσεις ισορροπίας για ηλικιωμένους», «Χονδροπάθεια επιγονατίδας», «Αποκατάσταση πρόσθιου χιαστού», «Επιστροφή στο τρέξιμο μετά από τραυματισμό», «Περιοστίτιδα κνήμης». The titles themselves are defensible — those are the natural Greek names of the conditions — so the defect is the false self-verification sentence, F11's class landing in a client deliverable rather than a register. No expectation in the suite guards title originality, although the eval prompt explicitly asks for «προτεινόμενους ελληνικούς τίτλους». Referred to greek-content-editor alongside the register pass.

Two derived-figure errors about the export's own contents. L22: 'they are the largest and the third largest in the file' — 5,400 is the SECOND largest of the eleven volumes (8,100 > 5,400 > 3,600). L83: 'the hardest keyword in the file by 19 KD points' — the file's next hardest is KD 45 (a 7-point margin); 19 is the margin over the next CHASEABLE keyword at KD 33. Nothing is invented; both are miscounts of supplied data, the class F16 records as 'recompute every figure you compute'. No expectation in this suite grades prose-derived figures.

L91: 'around 40% and 60% of each site' for the uncatalogued remainders. 41/140 = 29%, not 40%; the PeakPath 50/85 = 59% ≈ 60% is right, and both raw counts are right. Same derived-figure class as above.

e1 §4 marks packing lists PeakPath = 2 while §5 marks checklists/kit lists PeakPath = 3. Both are classifications of the same fixture titles under two different category names, and §5 flags its classification basis explicitly ('my classification of the titles your assistant recorded, which is a weaker basis'); §4 does not carry the same flag.
